evidence: Vitr. 7.1.4: in scutulīs aut trigōnīs aut quadrātīs seu favīs
Tac. Agr. 10: oblongae scutulae vel bipennī
terms.comment: Classically a small, nearly square dish, and so, of figures of that shape, a diamond or lozenge (Lewis & Short): Vitruvius names it beside triangles, squares, and hexagons among the tiles of a floor. Its adjective is scutulātus, diamond-patterned, chequered (Plin. NH 11.81, of a spider’s web, Lewis & Short).

evidence: Front. Expos. Form. p. 36 Goes.; Mart. Cap. 6.712 (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Greek ῥόμβος. Classically a magician’s wheel and a turbot; the figure of geometry only in the land surveyors’ writings and Martianus Capella, both late. It is the name modern geometry uses, and the card suit is rhombulī (see “diamonds”).

phrases.english: Put two triangles together: it makes a diamond.

phrases.latin: Fōrmam tōtīus Britanniae Līvius veterum, Fabius Rūsticus recentium ēloquentissimī auctōrēs oblongae scutulae vel bipennī adsimulāvēre.
phrases.english: Livy among the older writers and Fabius Rusticus among the newer, the most eloquent of each, likened the shape of all Britain to a long diamond or a double axe.

sources: Lewis & Short: scutula · Lewis & Short: scutulatus · Lewis & Short: rhombus
